Whoa, Why does it pulse like that?

When the bottle explodes a gas bubble is formed and expands outward. As it expands, the gas pressure begins to drop. Once it has expanded enough, the outside water pressure becomes higher than the bubble's internal pressure and is able to push back in. It does so and starts collapsing the bubble. As this collapses happens the gas' pressure starts going up. This goes on until the gas once again is dense enough to overcome the water pressure. The bubble rebounds and starts pushing the water back out again.

Wash, rinse, repeat until the bubble is able to make it to the surface or other forces overcome this action. You can see in the video that with each repeat the amount of force is smaller. There is also less force from the above water acting on the bubble the closer it gets to the surface, so it can get bigger each time.

My real answer is cars. My grandfather used to buy them new all the time. He wasn't rich, but this was much easier in those days. 30's-70's American cars are awesome. New ones are great too, but to be able to be the first guy to drive a 54 Eldorado or a 38 Cadilac Coupe or something like that would be awesome. And everyone took pride in their cars. They could do simple repairs and knew the stats and terminology, and cleaned and waxed and maintained them, and on the weekends, cruised up and down the new Boulevards and Parkways, build specifically for the purpose of pleasure cruising. New drive-in destinations like movies and diners; car-hops became a sought-after summer job. People drove places just to cruise around. National parks were re-designed for pleasure cruising. Cars that they don't even make today, like Packard and LaSalle and Hurst and AMC - there were dozens! Many had some serious clout, but when the war came, those that didn't immediately change over to war-time production slowly died off, never to return. That would be cool to see though - the golden age of the American automobile.

And speaking of war - the same grandfather was in the Korean war. Non-combat - he built bridges. But really, Korea was the last "real war" which I think is a huge thing. Vietnam started the guerrilla wars - tactical, dirty practices, chemical bombs, napalm, agent orange, little skirmishes here and there, but no real all out war. Not saying that's good or bad, it just makes me wonder. There was more honor then.

That's an important distinction, on the war, isn't it? Especially now that we're moving into so many autonomous and robotic things.

...I hate to ask, but what's the internet merit badge for?

(I'll date myself here...) When I was in scouts, they didn't have it. It was a HUGE controversy when they added it and a few others since the scouts I was raised in did all the traditional Andy Griffith sorts of stuff. Here's a bunch of manly men, cutting down trees with their dicks and making parkas from the still bleeding skins of Bigfoot, and the scouts told them they had to go inside and turn on a computer. Today it seems like a laughable IN SOVIET RUSSIA, but seriously, it happened. What really started that push and gave it traction were the radio guys. Radio has always been the scouting gateway drug into technology because, at very least, the camps all had HAM radios. The HAM radios always had an uncomfortable following with the Morse code and signalling guys. And since Morse code is somehow kosher, and blah blah blah safety and insurance, and HAM used to be heavily regulated so it required merit badge sorts of training, the HAM guys brought in the PC technology under the auspices of signalling. OK that's cool back in the BBS days, and part of that merit badge in my heyday was identifying a modem and computer parts and actually getting a modem to connect to a BBS, but then the internet happened and the scouts had a real crisis.

The internet is important, BUT it's not regulated like HAM stuff! How do we merit badge it?

This is where my personal observations get a bit lost. The scouts weren't modernizing it, my father was deployed, and my mother wanted some group to teach the kids how to live in the office and not the woods, so she pulled me and my brother out.

These days it's managed to reform itself: http://www.scouting.org/Home/BoyScouts/AdvancementandAwards/MeritBadges/mb-DIG_TECH.aspx

Step 6F is one of the ones I recognize from the "old" badge, when this was actually a pain in the ass. But all of Step 6 is really that situation I'm describing where they have to figure out some way to keep the theme in the face of the new technology. You can see the backwards and forwards looking things in that list. Some of it is actually pretty useful such as the patent portions and IP bits. I would like to see them continue the trend with things like identity theft knowledge. We bag on it because it seems goofy but they really do try to keep it useful.

I still haven't actually approached them, but make casual conversation, sort of, with people out on walks, when I'm gardening; I also have a neighbor down the street who I knew from work before she left, so that's something. But, in every other instance, other than when I was very, very young, neighbors have always just been... weird and argumentative.
